cim: Artificial intelligence and authentic infuriation: The growing healthcare divide
cim_eredeti: Artificial intelligence and authentic infuriation: The growing healthcare divide
szoveg_eredeti:
As artificial intelligence promises to revolutionise healthcare, the disconnect between technological advances and patients’ lived experiences is fuelling frustration, anger and violence, writes Simon Tatz.

INFURIATION, frustration, anger and violence against healthcare workers and other frontline staff is escalating.

The expectation that artificial intelligence (AI) is making our lives easier and simpler contrasts with individual reality and experience, and this incongruence is manifesting in truly disturbing breakdowns of societal norms.

Like shifting tectonic plates, these two conflicting narratives are colliding, and the shockwaves are being felt, literally, by health and services sector workers.

A major study into violence against healthcare workers noted a salient factor:

‘Patient's expectations of access, expediency and efficacy of care appear to have increased, as health information has proliferated.’

Artificial expectations collide with authentic reality.

Patients are turning to chatbots before therapy and our mental healthcare systems aren't ready for it.

Reports of physical and verbal attacks are frightening, and I’m not on the front line going to work fearful of assaults and abuse by a public whose infuriation has become vicious.

The rise in healthcare workers being assaulted has, according to the Australasian College for Emergency Medicine (ACEM):

‘...more than doubled in the past decade, and assault is now the second leading cause of injury hospitalisation in this workforce. More than 7,400 health care workers have been hospitalised for a work-related injury in the past ten years, including 819 in 2024–25 alone.’

In Victoria, the Coalition’s response to almost 24,000 “violent incidents” recorded in the State’s health services (2024/25) is to fund 70 armed Protective Services Officers (PSOs) in major Victorian hospitals.

Aberrantly, AI is a contributing factor in the violence and infuriation towards those seen as the “face” of failing health services.

I postulate this because AI is widening the chasms between existing systems and structures and the (as yet) fully realised potential for AI to deliver the seismic improvements the public demands, especially from health services.

Australia’s health architecture is built on structures, systems, processes and beliefs created in a bygone era; mostly by men instilled with concepts founded in 19th-century Britain.

As Australia was settled, we followed the British model of building hospitals, then smaller primary care, specialist and allied health clinics, and demanding those needing healthcare find their own way to these services.

The Coalition must do more to prioritise the health of nurses who are turning away from the profession at the worst possible time due to burn-out, stress and insufficient resources.

With some notable exceptions – the Royal Flying Doctor Service and outreach care – this is how the Australian health system has functioned for almost 200 years.

Then AI arrived as a panacea; lauded as the solution to historic inequities, geographic and socio-economic barriers, and traditional inefficiencies.

AI, we’re told repeatedly (often by AI-assisted social media posts, reports and articles), is revolutionising healthcare.

The tyranny of distance is overcome via Telehealth and remote monitoring; ePrescribing transforms paper-based systems; patients benefit from automation of clinical documentation; AI scribes, AI diagnostic imaging and faster, more personalised health care are here, and the benefits are real.

And apps galore. There’s an app for every condition, problem or wellbeing angst.

Technology is outpacing us every day; therefore, we must be benefiting from it.

The narrative driven by AI conflicts with another narrative — our personal experience, circumstance and what we learn from public discourse.

There’s a crisis in mental health, especially youth mental health.

There’s a crisis within the mental health crisis around psychiatrists’ fees and availability, scope of practice and the rise of unregulated AI chatbots.

There’s a crisis in aged care and a crisis in aged care bed availability.

Australia is experiencing a healthcare workforce crisis.

Victoria's failing mental health system is leaving its most vulnerable without the care, safety and compassion they desperately need.

Regional and rural communities struggle with GP and specialist shortage crises.

A digital health skills crisis is hindering workforce advancement.

First Nations health has been in crisis since colonisation.

The immigration debate is another crisis.

AI and apps aren’t alleviating these media-enhanced crises; oftentimes they exacerbate them.

The “worried well” are overwhelming health services with “issues” derived from apps, social media influences and fear of missing out on the latest that health technology offers.

Knowledge about health innovations and interventions increases demand for services, which arguably suppresses the needs of those least able to afford and access healthcare.

The collision between these narratives is infuriating.

How do you comprehend a health system being transformed by AI at the same time it’s often failing at the most basic structural and service levels — access, affordability and equity?

We recognise this dichotomy when we’re confronted with the health system.

Patients are increasingly less patient. We’re aware of the massive advances in diagnostic tools, enhanced health data and information, essential health apps and telehealth.

We’re aware, too, of experience: long waiting times, increasing out-of-pocket costs and (in)continuity of care when they constantly see different GPs.

We’re aware of Australia’s antiquated system that requires a GP consult to obtain or renew a referral to see a specialist.

AI hype conceals corporate failures, deflects accountability and fuels fears of job losses to undermine workers’ bargaining power.

Scope of Practice reviews and inquiries haven’t delivered the structural changes that mirror AI advances.

The popularity of health chatbots furthers these competing narratives. How is it that a friendly, compliant chatbot can listen to you and diagnose your condition almost instantly, yet it can take weeks to book an appointment with a GP?

How can AI be positively improving our health system, reducing clinical errors, producing better measured outcomes while the healthcare workforce appears increasingly burnt out, under-resourced and under attack? Literally.

We struggle to reconcile these conflicting narratives — rapid advances created by AI while confused by a Byzantine health structure that is antiquated and unhelpful.

My best analogy is vehicle transport, where expensive, AI-assisted cars are steered by drivers outraged at potholes and deteriorating road surfaces.

As with healthcare, AI-based improvements in vehicle technology have accompanied a rise in deaths and road trauma. Australia’s road toll has been increasing since 2020 along with incidents of road rage.

Vehicles get better while drivers become angrier, more distracted, less capable and more intolerant. It’s why potholes were a major election issue in Victoria — these two narratives needed to blame someone.

Terrifyingly, we’re seeing frustration in healthcare, like road rage, quickly escalate to violence and aggression.

Australia is being rapidly transformed by AI, as mental health, aged care, hospitals and affordable access to the right medical care are seemingly getting worse and harder to access.

Simon Tatz was Director of Communications, Mental Health Australia and Director of Policy, Mental Health Victoria.
